---
title: "Ownership and Move Semantics"
description: "One key Rust idea, one tiny executable example, the reason it works, and a precise pitfall."
---

## The question

**Why doesn't assigning one String simply make two independent owners?**

A String owns a heap allocation. Assigning it to another variable normally moves that ownership; the old binding can no longer be used.

## The core rule

String moves; integer types such as i32 implement Copy, so their values are duplicated.

## One complete example

Paste these lines into `main.rs` and run with `rustc --edition 2024 main.rs && ./main`, or [use the tested Rust examples project](examples/index.qmd).

~~~rust
fn main() {
    let a = String::from("hello");
    let b = a;             // ownership moves to b
    println!("{b}");       // hello
    // println!("{a}");    // does not compile: a moved
}
~~~

**Walk through it:** The binding `a` is no longer allowed to access its old allocation after the move. The allocation is freed when its current owner (`b`) goes out of scope. No garbage collector is required for this ordinary owned value.

## Mathematical model — explained with real values

$$
owners(v)=1
$$

**What every symbol means:** `owners(v)` is a teaching shorthand for the number of active owning bindings to one non-`Copy` value `v`. Rust enforces one current owner in ordinary ownership moves; this shorthand is not a complete formal memory model.

**Substitute actual values:** At first, the `String` allocation belongs to `a` (one owner). After `let b = a`, ownership moves to `b` (still one owner), not two. An explicit `clone()` creates **another value** with another allocation.

## Common misunderstanding

What if you need both Strings? Use `let b = a.clone();` to explicitly allocate a second owned String. A `let x = 3; let y = x;` assignment is different because `i32` is `Copy`.

## Remember it in one sentence

String moves; integer types such as i32 implement Copy, so their values are duplicated.

**Official reference:** [The Rust Programming Language / Rust Reference](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-01-what-is-ownership.html).
